paras: The arrest of Mabel Puffer and Arthur Hazzard took place in Concord, New Hampshire, in June 1919, when Massachusetts officials arrested Mabel Emeline Puffer, a white woman of Ayer, Massachusetts, and her fiancé Arthur Garfield Hazzard, a Black man, shortly before their planned wedding and took both to Boston. Hazzard was held on a statutory charge later described as enticement, and Puffer on an insanity warrant sworn out by a niece. By July 11 the charges against Hazzard had been dropped and a court had declared Puffer insane, an outcome the Chicago Defender headlined "Prejudice Wins Out in Intermarriage Case."

Puffer, 48, was described as a woman of considerable wealth with a summer home at Sandy Pond and a former public reader and teacher. A Boston Chronicle account reprinted in the Baltimore Afro-American reported that the couple had left Ayer together and applied for a marriage license in Concord. According to the same account, the Concord police chief telephoned the Ayer chief of police, said he had no legal grounds to interfere, and suggested that Puffer's relatives take action.

Interviewed in Concord, both denied that they had eloped, Hazzard denied that he was marrying for money, and Puffer told her Ayer attorney, George L. Wilson, that there was no distinction of color. A Christian Scientist, she held that differences of color and age did not matter, and the Defender noted that New Hampshire had no law against intermarriage.

A Defender dispatch from Concord dated June 27 said both were arrested "last week" at the Phoenix Hotel, Hazzard on the hotel steps as he was about to buy a newspaper and Puffer as she was preparing to go to supper with him. The warrants were issued by a judge whose name the papers print as Atwood, Alwood and Mawood; the complainants were the town authorities of Ayer and, on the insanity warrant, Puffer's niece, Mrs. Mary L. Goodwin. The couple were then driven to Boston, the Defender writing that a car "was waiting outside, and before an attorney could be secured to halt the kidnappers she was spirited out of town."

In Boston, Hazzard retained William H. Lewis, a former assistant United States district attorney, who called the case "pure camouflage" and "a brazen persecution without foundation" meant to prevent the marriage. The judge ordered two physicians to examine Puffer, and one of them, Dr. Frank S. Balkley (white), was quoted as saying "She is as same [sane] as we are." Hazzard was released on bail, given later as $300, while Puffer was denied bail and kept in custody.

In early July the Defender reported that Puffer was confined pending a jury trial on her mental responsibility and had received letters with marriage offers from white men and threats against Hazzard. She told a Defender reporter that the effort to have her adjudged insane was meant to separate them.

On July 11 the Defender reported from Ayer that the statutory charges against Hazzard had been dropped after Lewis and associate counsel C. J. O'Neill of Lowell appeared for him, and that the court had declared Puffer insane. A companion report said her family intended to send her to California to keep her from Hazzard, and that it was rumored she had never been properly examined by alienists. When the verdict was given, Puffer was quoted as saying, "It's too bad that in this so-called free counsellor [country] people can't marry whom they love."

Among Black weeklies, the Baltimore Afro-American ran the Boston Chronicle's pre-arrest story on June 27 under the headline "Wealthy White Woman, Determined To Marry Colored Sweetheart," with a deck ending "Wish Them Luck." The Chicago Defender put the case on its front page three weeks running, on June 28, July 5 and July 12.

Its language treated the arrests as a seizure: it wrote of "the kidnappers," printed Lewis's charge of persecution, ran its own interview with Puffer, and headlined the outcome "Prejudice Wins Out in Intermarriage Case at Boston, Mass."
Hazzard's age differs between the two papers: the Afro-American's account made him 33, "15 years her junior," while the Defender gave his age as 38.

reader.title: Arrest of Mabel Puffer and Arthur Hazzard
bases: The papers describe an arrest of an interracial couple on warrants by Massachusetts officials and an insanity proceeding against the white bride, not a mob attack; the Defender calls the arresting party 'kidnappers' but reports no physical violence (A3, A4, A8).

The arrests, charges and outcome are reported only by the Chicago Defender across three weekly issues (A3, A4, A8); the Afro-American's Boston Chronicle account (A1, A2) predates the arrests and confirms only the couple and the license application.
